transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I... gosh, where do I even start? I suppose I came in because I just seem to be worrying about absolutely everything now. And I mean everything. I'm a real estate broker, you see, and I know the market fluctuates—that's just the nature of the business, I've been doing it a long time—but lately, I am just agonizing over my clients, the state of the market, every little detail. 

But it doesn't stop with work. It spills over into my personal life, too. I worry constantly about my family, about our money situation... we actually just recently moved into a condo, which was supposed to simplify things, you know? Downsizing, less maintenance, that whole idea. But instead of just settling in and enjoying it, I just keep obsessing over whether moving to the condo was actually the right decision. I mean, what if the association fees skyrocket? What if we made a huge mistake and we're stuck? 

And I know, logically, I know it feels completely out of proportion to what is actually happening. Things are generally fine! But my mind just takes these everyday things and spins them into these massive, overwhelming concerns, and I just can't seem to stop doing it. It's just constant.
Do you find yourself repeating certain actions or thoughts over and over as a way to cope with these worries?

No, no, not really. I mean, I don't have any, like, routines or rituals, if that's what you're asking. I know some people, they get anxious and they have to clean the entire house or check the locks five times. My sister-in-law is actually a bit like that, bless her heart, she has to check the garage door every single time she leaves the house, sometimes twice. But for me, it’s not like I’m doing a specific action to make the worry go away. I honestly wish I had something that made it go away! 

Instead, I just... I just sit in it. The thoughts themselves just loop, but not on purpose, and certainly not to cope. Like, I’m not repeating a mantra or anything helpful like that. I’ll just be sitting at the kitchen island—we have this beautiful new quartz island in the condo, which was supposed to be where my husband and I would drink our morning coffee and just finally relax at this stage in our lives—and I'll just be staring into my mug, completely paralyzed by the thought of the housing market crashing, or the HOA board deciding to replace the roof and hitting us with some massive special assessment. 

And my husband, he’ll come into the kitchen and say, "You're a million miles away again," and I realize I've just been sitting there for twenty minutes letting the worry completely take over. I just run through every worst-case scenario. So, no, I wouldn't say I do anything over and over to cope with it. I don't really feel like I'm coping at all, to be honest. I just sort of let the worries run rampant in my head until I completely exhaust myself.
Do you ever feel a strong urge to perform a specific behavior or mental act in response to your worries?

No, not an urge, really. I think... well, it's just like what I was trying to explain a moment ago. I don't have this sudden, overwhelming need to do something to fix the thought. Not physically, and not mentally either. I know you mentioned a mental act, like maybe counting in my head or repeating a specific phrase to cancel out the bad thought? I don't do anything like that. 

I really just get stuck. It’s funny you ask that specific question, though, because I was actually just telling my friend Susan about this—she’s another broker at my firm, we've worked together for over fifteen years, practically raised our kids together—and I was telling her that when the worry hits about the market or the condo fees, I don't spring into action. I don't have an urge to go balance my checkbook or run numbers in my head to soothe myself, which you'd think a real estate agent would do! 

If anything, the worry just paralyzes me. Like yesterday, I had this whole stack of closing documents for a lovely young couple—first-time buyers, so they're already incredibly nervous, which usually I'm great at handling because I've been doing this since the late 80s—but I started worrying about their inspection report and what might go wrong with their loan, and instead of having an urge to double-check the paperwork or organize my desk to feel in control, I just sat there. I just sat at the table letting the scenarios play out. My husband even asked if I was going to finish reviewing the file, and I just couldn't snap out of the worry. 

So, no, there's no urge to *do* anything, physical or mental, to respond to it. It's just a heavy, heavy blanket of 'what ifs' that I can't shake off. I really wish there was some little mental trick or action I could just do to make it stop, but there isn't. I just sort of suffer through the spiral.
Do you have any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to ignore them?

Yes, oh absolutely. That is exactly what happens, and it is incredibly frustrating because I really do try to ignore them. I try so hard to just push them out of my head. 

Like just the other night, we were sitting down to watch Jeopardy in the new living room. My husband loves Jeopardy, we have watched it together every weeknight for years, it is just our little routine to decompress. And I was really trying to focus on the trivia and just unwind, but my brain was just completely stuck on an email I had sent to a title company earlier that afternoon. I kept telling myself, Parin, this is not urgent. The title company is closed, the escrow officer is at home with her family, nobody is even going to look at this until at least nine o'clock tomorrow morning. 

But it just does not matter what I tell myself, or how hard I try to just watch the television. One concern just leads right into another. I start wondering if I missed a signature line on the addendum, and then I start worrying that the appraisal is going to come in low, and then what if the buyers decide to walk away entirely and lose their earnest money... and before I know it, the show is completely over and I have spent half an hour replaying all these small details I meant to let go. 

I try to ignore them, I really do, but they just hijack my brain anyway. It is like a train that just takes off without me, and I can be sitting right there on the sofa next to my husband, but in my mind, I am miles away just going over and over the same worries.
Do you feel like these repeating thoughts are trying to get you to do something or fix something in your mind?

No, no, I wouldn't say they're trying to get me to fix anything, really. It's not like... it's not a productive feeling, if that makes sense. Like, if I have a thought about fixing something, it's usually, "Oh, I need to call the plumber about the guest bathroom sink," and then I go and call the plumber, or at least write it down on the notepad I keep by the phone in the kitchen. We had this terrible leak a few years ago in our old house before we downsized to the condo, ruined the hardwood floors in the hallway, so I am very on top of plumbing issues now! 

But these thoughts, the ones that just keep looping and looping... they aren't like that. They aren't asking me to solve a problem. They're just... they're just pure worry. It's not my brain saying, "Parin, you need to go double-check that contract right now." It's more like my brain saying, "What if the contract falls through and the clients hate you and your reputation is ruined and the market crashes and we can't afford the condo fees?" There's nothing to *fix* in that scenario, you know? It's just a cascade of terrible possibilities. 

I'm not trying to solve a puzzle in my head, or figure out a way to make everything okay. I'm just trapped in the 'what ifs.' Like with the HOA board—I can't fix the roof myself, I can't control what they decide to assess us for, so the thoughts aren't driving me to an action or a solution. They're just spinning. It's exhausting, honestly, because if they *were* trying to get me to fix something, maybe I could just fix it and be done with it! But there's no fixing it, there's just... enduring it until my brain finally decides it's tired of that particular worry and moves on to something else.
Do you feel like you must think about these worries or repeat them in your mind, even if you don't want to?

Well, it's not that I feel like I *must* think about them... it's not a compulsion, if that's what you mean. It's more like I just *can't stop* thinking about them. It's not a choice I'm making, like, "Oh, I really need to sit down and worry about the escrow account for the Smith property for the next forty-five minutes." I don't want to think about it at all! 

Like I was saying about Jeopardy, I want to watch the show. I want to relax. My husband, bless him, he retired a few years ago—he was an engineer, very black and white, very logical—and he just cannot understand why I can't just turn it off. He'll say, "Parin, just leave work at work," and I try to explain to him that I'm not choosing to bring it home. It just follows me. 

So, no, I don't feel a need to repeat them on purpose, or like I'm required to think about them. They just force their way in. It's like having a radio playing in the background of your mind, and the dial is stuck on a station that only broadcasts bad news, and the volume knob is broken. You don't *want* to listen to it, and you're not choosing to tune in, but it's blaring so loudly that you can't hear anything else. You're just subjected to it, no matter how much you'd rather be listening to silence, or, you know, Alex Trebek—well, Ken Jennings now, I suppose, though it took us a while to get used to the change! But yes, it's not a 'must,' it's just a 'can't help it.'
Do you feel like these worries are unwanted and are invading your mind?

Well, yes and no. I mean, they are definitely unwanted, absolutely. Like I said, I would love nothing more than to just sit and enjoy my evening without my brain running through every possible disaster scenario with my clients or the HOA or whatever else it decides to latch onto. So in that sense, yes, I do not want them there.

But "invading"? I don't know if that's the right word for it. It's not like they feel like some foreign entity or something alien putting thoughts into my head. It's still *my* brain, you know? It's just my brain working overtime. It's my own voice in my head, my own concerns, just... amplified and out of control. 

It's not like when you get a pop-up ad on your computer that comes out of nowhere and takes over the screen. It's more like... well, it's like I'm the one typing the search terms into Google, but my fingers won't stop typing, and it just keeps pulling up more and more terrible results. It's my own thought process, just spinning its wheels. 

I was talking to my sister about this last weekend—she lives out in Arizona, retired teacher, very different personality from me, much more laid back. And she was saying, "Parin, you just have to learn to shut the door on those thoughts." And I told her, it's not like someone is knocking on the door trying to get in. The thoughts are already inside the house! They're just pacing around the living room and refusing to sit down. So they are definitely unwanted, but they don't feel like an invasion from outside. They just feel like a part of me that I can't quite get a handle on.
Are these worries affecting your ability to function at work or in your personal relationships?

Well, yes, they are... they're definitely getting in the way, especially at work. It's so frustrating because I've been doing this for over thirty years. I know the real estate market in this area like the back of my hand, and I've always prided myself on being efficient and sharp. But lately... oh, it's just exhausting. 

Even the most straightforward things, like listing negotiations or reviewing a standard contract, are taking me so much longer than they used to. I’ll sit there staring at a clause that I’ve read a thousand times before, and my brain will just start spinning with all those 'what ifs.' What if I missed a contingency? What if the buyer's financing falls through because of some tiny error I didn't catch? What if I'm advising my client poorly and they end up losing the house? 

And because I'm so caught up in making sure every single little detail is absolutely perfect to prevent these imaginary disasters, I find myself rereading the same documents over and over again. It's slowing me down terribly. I've even had to delay returning calls to clients or other agents because I just don't feel confident that I've checked everything carefully enough yet. I'll tell myself, "Just let it go to voicemail, Parin, you need another ten minutes to review the inspection report," but then ten minutes turns into thirty, and I'm still agonizing over it. 

It's embarrassing, frankly. My husband tells me I'm overworking myself, but it's not that I have more work to do, it's that the work I *do* have is taking me twice as long because of all this worrying! So, yes, it's definitely affecting my ability to function at work the way I'm used to.
Do you feel like these worries are causing you a lot of distress?

Well, yes, I suppose distress is a good word for it. It's just... it's very upsetting to feel this way, you know? Like I was saying about the contracts taking so long, it's not just the time it takes, it's how I feel while I'm doing it. My stomach gets all tied up in knots, and I just feel this heavy, sinking feeling in my chest. 

I've always been the kind of person who handles things. When the market crashed back in 2008, I was the one keeping our office afloat, figuring out short sales, calming down panicked sellers... I thrived on it, really. I was the steady one. And now? Now I'm the one who feels like she's constantly on the verge of a panic over a standard home inspection! 

It's just so frustrating to feel like my own mind is working against me. I'll be sitting at my desk, looking out the window—I have a lovely view of the oak trees in the courtyard from my office—and instead of appreciating it, I'm just sitting there feeling completely overwhelmed by these thoughts. And it makes me so tired. Not just sleepy-tired, but a deep, bone-weary kind of exhaustion from just constantly battling my own brain. 

My husband sees it, too. He'll come into the kitchen while I'm making dinner, and he can tell just by looking at my shoulders that I'm wound up tight as a spring. I'll be chopping onions or something, and I'm not even thinking about the recipe, I'm just agonizing over whether I worded an email to a client correctly three hours ago. It takes the joy out of things. I used to love cooking, trying out new recipes from those magazines I subscribe to, but now it just feels like another chore to get through while my mind races. So, yes, it's very distressing. It's just not how I want to live my life, especially not now, when things should be settling down and getting easier!
Are these worries affecting your relationships with your family or friends?

Well, with my husband, like I mentioned when I was talking about making dinner, he definitely feels the brunt of it because I'm just so tense and not really present with him. But with my friends... honestly, I feel like I'm neglecting them entirely. 

I've been in a book club with the same group of women for, oh, it has to be fifteen years now. We meet on the first Tuesday of every month, usually at this nice little bistro downtown, and it's always been a priority for me. But lately, I've been showing up an hour late or just canceling on them at the last minute. 

And I know I keep going back to my job, and I know I already brought this up, but that's really where it hits my personal relationships the hardest. Because, like I was saying before, at work, even the most straightforward listing negotiations and contract reviews are taking me *so* much longer than they used to. I’ll be sitting at my desk at 5:30 when I’m supposed to be heading out to meet Susan and the rest of the girls, and I’m stuck there. I've had to delay returning calls to clients or other agents because I just don't feel confident I've checked everything carefully enough, so I end up staying at the office until seven or eight at night just rereading the same lines of text. 

I'll think to myself, "I can't go sit and enjoy a glass of Pinot Noir and talk about a novel when I might have missed a contingency date on page four." So I stay late, and I miss out on my friends. They're polite about it, of course, they always say they understand that the real estate market is demanding, but I know it's straining things. Susan even made a little comment last week about how I'm married to my brokerage these days. It hurts to hear that, because it’s not that I *want* to be missing out on my life! It’s just that I can't pull myself away to be a good friend or a relaxed wife when I'm so consumed by this fear that I haven't been careful enough with my files.
Are you finding it difficult to meet your responsibilities at work or at home due to these worries?

Well, yes, and I know I probably sound like a broken record at this point, constantly bringing it back to the office, but that’s really where I’m feeling the weight of it the most as far as my actual day-to-day responsibilities go. Like I was telling you just a moment ago, it’s those straightforward listing negotiations and reviewing the standard contracts that are just taking me so much longer than they ever used to. I mean, I’ve been doing this for over three decades, I should be able to process these files in my sleep! 

But instead, I’m falling behind on my duties. I’ve had to delay returning calls to my clients and to other agents—which is a terrible practice in real estate, time is completely of the essence in this market—but I just keep putting those calls off because I simply don’t feel confident that I’ve checked everything carefully enough to give them the go-ahead. I’ll look at the phone ringing, know it’s a buyer's agent waiting for an answer, and I just let it ring because I’m still second-guessing a disclosure form from three days ago. So my professional responsibilities are definitely taking a massive hit, which is completely out of character for me. 

And then at home, well, it spills over there, too. Because I'm so behind at work from all this checking and re-checking, I'm really not doing my share around the house anymore. My husband has been doing the grocery shopping and most of the cooking lately, because I'm either staying at the brokerage until all hours trying to catch up, or I'm physically sitting in our living room but I'm completely checked out, just too drained from agonizing over whether I made a mistake on a contract to even help him load the dishwasher. It's just... it's really hard to keep up with what I'm supposed to be doing anywhere right now, and it makes me feel like I'm failing at both ends.
Are there specific tasks or activities that you've stopped doing altogether because of your worries?

Well, no, not altogether. I haven't completely stopped doing anything, per se. It's more like everything I do is just... tainted by it, I suppose. 

Like I said, I'm still going to work, I'm still sitting at my desk, I'm still technically reviewing the contracts and doing the negotiations, even if it's taking me three times as long and I'm missing my book club to do it. I haven't just thrown my hands up and walked out of the brokerage, although heaven knows there are days when I'm staring at a stack of disclosures and I certainly feel like I want to! I've been a broker for thirty-two years, I couldn't just walk away. It's too much a part of who I am. 

And at home, I haven't stopped... well, I mean, I told you my husband is doing more of the cooking and the shopping right now, but I haven't stopped trying to be a part of the household. I still try to make dinner on the weekends when things are a little slower, even if I'm standing there chopping vegetables and agonizing over whether I should have pushed harder for a seller's concession on the Johnson property. 

So, no, there isn't a specific task or activity that I've just completely crossed off my list and said, "I'm never doing this again because I'm too worried." It's more of a... a pervasive slowing down of everything. A hesitation. I'm still doing the things, I'm just doing them with this huge, heavy weight of doubt and fear dragging behind me every step of the way. It's exhausting, really, to keep pushing through it all, but I haven't stopped. Not yet, anyway.
Are there any situations or places that you're avoiding because of your worries?

Well, no, not avoiding places or situations entirely, no. Like I was just saying about the tasks, I haven't just shut myself in the house and refused to leave. I'm still going into the office every day. I mean, my office is right on Main Street, in this beautiful old Victorian building that we renovated about twelve years ago—it has these gorgeous bay windows and original hardwood floors. I love that office, I really do. I've spent more time there than in my own home over the last three decades! 

So, I'm still going there, even though, like I said, sitting at that desk right now just fills me with this immense dread about the contracts and the negotiations. And I'm still going out to show houses, too. Just last Thursday, I had to show a colonial over in the Heights—lovely neighborhood, great school district, always sells fast—and I went, I met the clients, I walked them through the property. But the whole time I was driving there, and walking through the rooms pointing out the crown molding, my mind was just racing, completely consumed with whether I'd properly filed the lead paint disclosure for a totally different listing. 

So I'm not avoiding going to the showings, or going to the office, or even going to the grocery store when I can actually pull myself away from work to do it. I'm still physically putting myself in all these situations. It's just that when I'm there, I'm not really *there*, if that makes sense. I'm present in body, but my mind is a million miles away, just spinning and spinning over all the things I might have missed or done wrong. I guess you could say I'm avoiding being mentally present, maybe? But physically, no, I'm still showing up to all the places I'm supposed to be, even if it feels like I'm dragging a hundred-pound weight with me everywhere I go.
Are you finding that your worries are causing you to withdraw from social interactions or activities that you once enjoyed?

Well, yes, I suppose I am, unfortunately. Like I briefly mentioned a few minutes ago about missing my book club... we usually meet on the first Tuesday of the month at this lovely little French bistro downtown, they have the most wonderful pastries, and I've been going with the same group of women for years. But lately, I've just been skipping it. And I haven't been to my weekend garden club meetings in probably a month and a half, either. 

But, you know, the real reason I'm withdrawing from all these social things I usually love always just comes right back to what I was telling you earlier about the office. I know I keep harping on it, but it's just consuming my entire schedule and my whole life, really. Because those straightforward listing negotiations and the standard contract reviews are taking me so much longer than they ever used to, I just don't have the time or the mental bandwidth for anything else. I'm stuck at my desk for hours agonizing over paperwork that should take me twenty minutes to approve. 

And the phone calls... I know I brought this up already, but it's really becoming such a massive problem. I'm having to delay returning calls to my clients and colleagues, just constantly putting them off, because I simply don't feel confident that I've checked everything carefully enough to speak to them. I'll get a voicemail from a buyer and think, 'Well, I can't call them back yet, I need to read page four of that inspection addendum just one more time to be absolutely sure I didn't miss a contingency.' 

So by the time I finally feel secure enough to actually pick up the phone and make the call, the whole day has slipped away. It's late, I'm completely drained, and the absolute last thing I want to do is go out and try to make small talk over a glass of wine. So, yes, I'm definitely pulling away from my social life, but it's really a direct domino effect from how much I'm struggling to just get through my basic, everyday work tasks.
Are you feeling like your worries are damaging your relationships with your loved ones?

Well, damaging might be a strong word, but... well, honestly, I'm not really sure if it's damaging them, per se. I haven't noticed any huge blowouts or anything like that. I mean, my husband, Richard, he's been an absolute saint through all of this. We've been married for thirty-eight years—our anniversary was actually just last month, we usually go up to this little bed and breakfast in Vermont, but this year we just stayed home because I couldn't bear the thought of being away from my email for a whole weekend. But anyway, Richard has been so patient. Like I mentioned before, he's taken over so much of the cooking and the grocery shopping, which he never used to do. He's a retired civil engineer, so he's very methodical, very organized, and he just steps in and handles things when he sees I'm overwhelmed. 

So, I wouldn't say my relationship with him is damaged. Strained, maybe? I know he worries about me when he sees me sitting at the kitchen island at eleven o'clock at night, still poring over a standard purchase agreement that I've already read five times. He'll come down in his robe and put a hand on my shoulder and say, "Elaine, it's time to put it away," and I just... I can't. And I know that frustrates him, even if he doesn't say it. 

And as for my kids, well, my daughter lives in Chicago and my son is in Denver, so we mostly just talk on the phone on Sundays. I suppose I haven't been as chatty or as engaged when they call. Usually, I'm asking all about my grandchildren—my daughter has two little ones, four and six, just the absolute lights of my life—but lately, when we're on the phone, I'm just so distracted. I'm nodding along and saying "uh-huh," but in my head, I'm trying to remember if I sent that addendum to the title company on Friday afternoon or if I just drafted the email and left it in my drafts folder. 

But they haven't said anything to me about it. They haven't complained that I'm being distant or anything. So, I don't know if I'd say the worries are actively damaging my relationships with them. It's more like... like I'm just not giving them my best self right now. I'm giving them whatever leftover scraps of energy I have after I've spent the whole week exhausting myself over work. But as for actual damage, like arguments or people pulling away from me? No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I just hope this doesn't go on so long that it *does* start to cause real problems, you know? Because family is everything to me, it really is. It's just that right now, the work... the worries about the work... they just seem to take up all the space in the room.
Are you having trouble completing tasks at home because of your worries?

Well, at home... honestly, like I was saying about Richard, he's really the one keeping the house running right now. So I suppose I'm not technically having trouble completing tasks at home, but mostly because I'm barely doing them! He's doing the dishes, he's handling the grocery shopping, bless his heart. But the reason I'm not doing those things around the house always, always comes back to what I was telling you earlier about my work. 

I know I keep circling back to this, and I apologize if I'm sounding like a broken record, but it really is the root of everything right now. The reason I can't even manage to, say, fold a load of laundry or water the houseplants is because my work tasks are just completely bleeding into every hour of my day. Like I mentioned before, it’s those straightforward listing negotiations and the standard contract reviews—things that used to be second nature to me after thirty years in this business! They are just taking me so, so much longer than they ever used to. I’ll bring the files home and spread them out all over the dining room table, and I just get entirely stuck. 

And I know I brought up the phone calls already, but that’s exactly how it plays out at home, too. I’ll be sitting there in the living room in the evening, knowing I need to call a buyer or a title agent back, and I just keep delaying returning the calls. I'll put it off for hours, just staring at my phone, because I just don’t feel confident that I’ve checked everything carefully enough. I'll think, 'Did I verify the earnest money deposit amount? Did I read the seller's disclosure twice?' I just have this overwhelming feeling that I missed something critical. So I'm sitting there re-reading the same paragraphs over and over instead of helping Richard with dinner or doing anything normal around the house, just because I can't bring myself to make a simple phone call until I'm absolutely, one hundred percent certain everything in the file is perfect. So the home tasks just completely fall by the wayside.
Are your worries significantly interfering with your ability to enjoy your daily life and maintain your relationships?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, like I’ve been saying—and I know I keep dragging us back to the exact same topic, I really do apologize for sounding like a broken record here—but it all just stems from the office. You ask about enjoying my daily life, and honestly, how can I? When every single day feels like I'm just wading through molasses. 

I know I've already told you about how those straightforward listing negotiations and the standard contract reviews are taking me so much longer than they ever used to. It’s just... it’s exhausting. It completely drains any joy I used to get out of my day. And because I get so bogged down in double and triple-checking every little clause, the whole schedule just collapses. 

Like I said before about the phone calls, I'm constantly having to delay returning calls to my clients and my colleagues. I'll sit there staring at the phone, knowing a buyer is waiting for an update on an inspection, but I just don't feel confident that I've checked everything carefully enough to actually speak to them. I feel like I have to read the addendum just one more time to be absolutely certain. And by the time I finally get through it all and make the call, the day is completely gone. 

There’s no time or energy left to just sit on the patio with Richard and have a glass of iced tea, or read a novel, or just relax like a normal person. My mind is just constantly trapped in those files. So, yes, it’s absolutely interfering with my ability to enjoy much of anything lately, because the worry about work just takes up all the oxygen in the room. I'm just so drained by the time I clock out that there's nothing left of me to actually enjoy my life.
Do you feel like your worries are a part of yourself or something that is happening to you against your will?

That is... well, that is a really interesting question, doctor. I am not sure I have ever really stopped to think about it in exactly those terms before. A part of myself versus against my will... hmm. I mean, on the one hand, I have been in real estate for thirty years, and you do not survive three decades in this business without being meticulous. I have always prided myself on being the kind of broker who dots every i and crosses every t. So being careful, thinking ahead, anticipating problems, that has always been a part of who I am. That is just me. But lately... well, lately it feels like that part of my personality has just completely taken the wheel and will not let me touch the brakes. 

So, is it happening against my will? I honestly do not know if I would use those exact words, because it is not like some sort of foreign entity has invaded my brain, you know? It is still my own thoughts. It is still me sitting there at the kitchen island at eleven at night. Richard is not forcing me to do it, my clients are not forcing me to do it, and half the time they do not even know I am up that late checking their files anyway. So I guess I am doing it to myself. 

But at the same time, I do not want to be doing it. I do not want to be staring at my phone, terrified to call a title agent back because I am doubting my own work. I want to just review a standard purchase agreement once, decide it looks fine, and go watch a movie with my husband. But I just cannot seem to stop the cycle once it starts. So I suppose I do not really have a clear, simple answer for you. It is my own mind, my own personality traits just magnified to a point where I feel like I am not entirely in control of them anymore. Does that make sense? I just do not know how to separate myself from the worry at this point, because it is all so tangled up in how I have always done my job.
Do you feel like these worries are in line with your own values and beliefs, or do they feel foreign to you?

Well, that’s... I guess that’s sort of tied up with what I was just trying to explain, isn’t it? About whether it’s me or against my will. As far as my values go... well, like I said, I’ve been in real estate for thirty years. Thirty years! You don't last that long, especially through all the market crashes and the bubbles and the sheer chaos of this industry, without having a very strong set of professional values. I believe in doing things right. I believe in protecting my clients. For a lot of these people, buying a house is the single biggest financial transaction of their entire lives, and they are trusting me to guide them through it. So my belief has always been that I owe them my absolute best, my complete attention to detail. I value integrity, I value thoroughness, and I value hard work.
